label: Landmark-based Shape Spaces
notes: This short chapter on printed pages 77 to 81 lays the foundation for the whole second part of the book. We define shape as what survives after removing nuisance transformations from a labelled landmark configuration, and we preview the quotient program that produces Kendall, reflection, affine, and projective shape spaces.

label: Configurations as Matrices
notes: A configuration of k labelled landmarks in m dimensions is stored as a k by m matrix, one row per point. Labelling matters: landmark i must mean the same anatomical or geometric feature across every specimen, otherwise correspondence is lost and no downstream shape comparison is meaningful.

label: What Is Shape?
notes: Shape is the geometric information left after we discard location, scale, and orientation. Two configurations have the same shape when one maps to the other by an allowed transformation. Choosing which transformations count as nuisance is a modelling decision that fixes exactly which shape space we build.

label: The Quotient Idea
notes: We let a transformation group act on configuration space and declare two configurations equivalent when they lie in the same orbit. Shape space is the set of orbits, the quotient of configuration space by the group. Each point of the quotient is one shape, represented by any member of its orbit.

label: Step 1: Remove Translation
notes: Subtracting the centroid from every landmark removes translation and centres the configuration at the origin. The centred configurations form a linear subspace of dimension k minus one times m. This is the first and least controversial quotient, applied universally before scale and rotation are addressed.

label: Step 2: Remove Scale
notes: Dividing the centred configuration by its Frobenius norm removes uniform scaling and places every specimen on a unit sphere, the pre-shape sphere. Pre-shape retains orientation but has fixed size and location, so only rotation still separates configurations that ought to share one shape.

label: Step 3: Remove Rotation
notes: Quotienting the pre-shape sphere by the rotation group collapses each rotational orbit to a single point and yields Kendall's similarity shape space. The orbits are circles or higher dimensional, and the quotient is generically a smooth manifold, although singular shapes can occur in low dimensions.

label: The Full Pipeline
notes: The complete program reads centre, then scale, then rotate: configuration to centred to pre-shape to shape. Each arrow removes one nuisance group and lowers dimension. Reading the diagram left to right shows equivalent configurations progressively collapsing until only intrinsic shape remains at the far right.

label: Choosing the Group
notes: Different choices of nuisance group give different shape spaces. Similarity uses rotations; reflection shape adds reflections; affine shape removes all invertible linear maps; projective shape removes projective transformations for camera views. The later chapters study each of these quotients and their distinct geometry in detail.

label: Manifolds and Singularities
notes: For generic landmark counts the shape space is a smooth Riemannian manifold, which is what makes nonparametric inference on it possible. In degenerate cases, such as collinear landmarks, orbits have smaller stabilizers and the quotient acquires singular points where the manifold structure breaks down.

label: Looking Ahead
notes: With shape defined as an orbit and shape space as a quotient manifold, we are ready to do statistics on it: intrinsic and extrinsic means, distances, and asymptotics. The next chapters realise Kendall, reflection, affine, and projective shape spaces concretely and develop inference tools for each.
